协作之林
自由
尚未

Collaboration 1. United labor, co-operation; esp. in literary, artistic, or scientific work. 2. Traitorous cooperation with the enemy.
协作（collaboration）：
1. 联合劳动，合作；尤指文学、艺术或科学工作。2. 与敌人的背叛性合作。
Freedom is elusive. It is easy to condemn any dream in hindsight. Yet there is something to say for delving into those bumbling moments of passion and empowerment when so much seems possible.
自由难以捉摸。事后贬斥任何梦想都很容易。然而，深入那些笨拙的激情与赋权时刻——那时如此之多似乎皆有可能——仍然有值得一说之处。

Freedom comes in many guises. The freedom of middle-class students to roam in wild nature contrasts with the struggle of activists for communal empowerment. Each of these in turn is barely in dialogue with the practical lives of forest residents, which depend on their ability to stay out of the way of the schemes of the ruling class. Can any cause for common justice emerge across these differences?
自由以多种面貌出现。中产阶级学生在野性自然中漫游的自由，与活动家争取社群赋权的斗争形成对比。这两者又都几乎不与森林居民的实际生活对话，而后者依赖于他们避开统治阶级计划的能力。跨越这些差异，能否出现任何共同正义的事业？

To ask this question well, we must move beyond the common-sense assumption that solidarity means homogeneity. Differences invigorate social mobilizations. Differences engage political abstractions, making them applicable to local situations. At the same time, differences are organized by common assumptions about political process. It is impossible to participate in a movement without representing one’s demands through its ruling discourses; no one unacquainted with the concept of freedom, for example, can make claims through it. Political mobilizations mount a generalized frame for what will count as politics, including the politics of difference. Difference is thus both a pre-established frame for connection and an unexpected medium in which connection must find local purchase.

要恰当地提出这个问题，我们必须超越“团结意味着同质”这一常识假设。差异使社会动员充满活力。差异让政治抽象概念参与进来，使其适用于当地情境。同时，差异由关于政治过程的共同假设组织。参与一场运动，不可能不通过其主导话语来表述自己的诉求；例如，不熟悉自由概念的人，无法通过它提出主张。政治动员为“什么算作政治”——包括差异的政治——搭起一个普遍化框架。因此，差异既是连接的预先建立的框架，也是连接必须在其中找到地方落点的意外媒介。

All this means that social mobilizations are facilitated by their appeal to diverse social groups, who find divergent means and meanings in the cause. Social mobilizations are also held up and redirected by their inclusion of varied groups, who disagree about what are supposed to be common causes and objects of concern. In this process, universalist causes are locally reconfigured, even as they are held by a wider-reaching charisma.
这一切意味着，社会动员因诉诸多样社会群体而得到推动，这些群体在事业中找到不同的手段和意义。社会动员也因纳入各种群体而受阻并改变方向，这些群体对什么是共同事业和关切对象意见不一。在这一过程中，普遍主义事业被地方性地重新配置，即使它们仍由一种影响更广的感召力维系。

One of the best places to look for this kind of friction is in the formation of collaborative objects, which draw groups into common projects at the same time as they allow them to maintain separate agendas. This chapter considers the formation of the community-managed forest as an object of advocacy. My narrative follows how a community-managed forest emerged in one time and place through the collaborative energies of village leaders in the Meratus Mountains of South Kalimantan, nature lovers from the provincial capital of Banjarmasin, and New Order-era national activists from the Indonesian capital, Jakarta. Meratus villagers, nature lovers, and activists are, of course, the three groups I have described in some detail in the preceding three chapters. As I have shown, each group has a rather different kind of commitment to nature. In this chapter, I mix up their separate stories to show what happened when these three separate commitments came together in a short—but productive—campaign. Quite against precedent, they succeeded, at least for a while, in establishing a landscape removed from corporate destruction because it could be considered a community-managed forest.

寻找这类摩擦的最佳地点之一，是协作对象的形成——这些对象把不同群体拉入共同项目，同时允许它们维持各自议程。本章考察作为倡导对象的社群管理森林的形成。我的叙述追随社群管理森林如何在特定时空，通过南加里曼丹梅拉图斯山脉的村庄领袖、省会班贾尔马辛的自然爱好者，以及来自首都雅加达的新秩序时代全国活动家的协作能量而出现。梅拉图斯村民、自然爱好者和活动家，当然就是我在前三章中较详细描述的三组人。如我所展示的，每一组对自然都有着相当不同的承诺。在本章中，我把他们各自的故事混合起来，展示当这三种分离的承诺在一场短暂却富有成效的运动中汇合时发生了什么。完全违背先例，他们成功地把一片地景从公司破坏中移出——至少暂时如此——因为它可以被视为社群管理的森林。

Yet this common object, the forest, did not just hold them together; it also kept them apart. For a historian of these events, one of the most striking things about the campaign is the fact that the varied, and equally satisfied, protagonists never came to any agreement about what happened. The coupling of obviously divergent perspectives and campaign success gives us pause. Activists are used to linking disagreement and failure; if participants disagree, we think the campaign must have been a mistake. In this campaign, undifferentiated unity was not a prerequisite for success.
然而，这个共同对象——森林——不只是把他们维系在一起；它也使他们彼此分离。对于这些事件的历史学家来说，运动最引人注目的一点在于，那些各执一词却同样满意的当事人，从未就发生了什么达成任何一致。明显分歧的视角与运动成功的结合令人驻足。活动家习惯于把分歧与失败联系起来；如果参与者意见不一，我们就认为运动一定出了错。在这场运动中，无差异的统一并不是成功的先决条件。

Difference within common cause: Perhaps this is more important than we ordinarily think. In this chapter I propose this kind of overlapping, linking difference as a model of the most culturally productive kinds of collaboration. This is not the most common connotation of collaboration; this is collaboration with a difference: collaboration with friction at its heart. Usually, scholars think of collaborators as like-minded colleagues who each contribute to a commonly conceived product. They are trained to be just alike before they begin to work together, so their collaboration is in itself culturally uneventful. Of course, there is another meaning of collaboration that opens the term in a different direction: Collaborators work with the enemy in wartime. These collaborators are not positioned in equality or sameness, and their collaboration does not produce a communal good. This is a place to start in opening up other meanings of working together. Parties who work together may or may not be similar and may or may not have common understandings of the problem and the product. The more different they are, the more they must reach for barely overlapping understandings of the situation. Their common cause is also a cultural encounter, and the objects on which they appear to agree are most successful when they appeal simultaneously to divergent cultural legacies. Furthermore, collaborators may or may not have any understanding of each other’s agendas. Such collaborations bring misunderstandings into the core of alliance. In the process, they make wide-ranging links possible: they are the stuff of global ties. They are also the stuff of emergent politics: they make new objects and agents possible.

共同事业中的差异：也许这比我们通常认为的更重要。在本章中，我提出这种重叠的、连接性的差异作为最具文化创造力的协作形式的一种模型。这不是协作最常见的含义；这是有差异的协作：以摩擦为核心的协作。通常，学者把合作者想象为志同道合的同事，各自为一个共同构思的产品作出贡献。他们在开始合作之前就被训练得彼此相似，因此他们的协作本身在文化上平淡无奇。当然，协作还有另一个含义，把这个词引向不同方向：合作者在战时与敌人合作。这些合作者并不处于平等或相同的位置，他们的协作不产生共同利益。这是打开“共同工作”其他含义的一个起点。共同工作的各方可能相似，也可能不相似；可能对问题和产品有共同理解，也可能没有。他们彼此差异越大，就越需要寻求对情势仅有少许重叠的理解。他们的共同事业也是一场文化遭遇，而他们似乎一致的对象，在同时诉诸不同文化遗产时最为成功。此外，合作者可能理解彼此的议程，也可能完全不理解。这类协作把误解带入联盟的核心。在这一过程中，它们使广泛的联系成为可能：它们是全球联系的原料。它们也是新兴政治的原料：它们使新的对象和行动者成为可能。

Community-based conservation—which depends upon such objects as community-managed forests—has become one of the most exciting agendas in environmentalist circles: to conservationists, it is the hope for on-the-ground environmental protection; to developers and social justice advocates, it returns environmentalist energies to people. At the same time, there is much to criticize in these projects, particularly in their peculiar reifications of forests, communities, and conservation. Before we follow either advocates or critics into naturalizing the object of their debates, it seems useful to ask how this object has, in various times and places, come into being. In at least one time and place, the collaborative process joined very different perspectives on people and forests; it succeeded in part because no one stopped to realize the depth of their disagreements. Collaboration was not consensus making but rather an opening for productive confusion. Productive confusion is sometimes the most creative and successful form of the collaborative production of natural and social objects—whatever their political status.

以社群为基础的保护——依赖于社群管理森林这类对象——已成为环保圈中最激动人心的议程之一：对保护主义者来说，它是实地环境保护的希望；对发展工作者和社会正义倡导者来说，它把环保主义能量归还给人民。同时，这些项目有许多可批评之处，尤其是它们对森林、社群和保护的奇特物化。在我们跟随倡导者或批评者把其辩论对象自然化之前，先问一问这个对象如何在不同的时间和地点形成，似乎是有益的。至少在一个时间和地点，协作过程把关于人与森林的非常不同的视角连接起来；它成功的部分原因在于没有人停下来意识到他们分歧的深度。协作不是达成共识，而是为富有成效的混淆打开空间。富有成效的混淆有时是自然与社会对象协作生产中最有创造性和最成功的形式——无论其政治地位如何。
Let me turn to the events.
让我转向事件本身。
What Happened in Manggur
芒古尔发生了什么

The small village of Manggur is located in the western foothills of the Meratus Mountains. The Meratus Dayak inhabitants are shifting cultivators and forest foragers. They are a small cultural minority in both the South Kalimantan region and the nation; most Indonesians, environmentalists or otherwise, have never heard of them. Yet in 1986 Manggur people played an important role in an environmentalist drama.
小村庄芒古尔位于梅拉图斯山脉西麓。梅拉图斯达雅克居民是游耕者和森林采集者。他们在南加里曼丹地区和国家都是一个小小的文化少数群体；大多数印尼人，无论是否环保主义者，从未听说过他们。然而1986年，芒古尔人在一出环保戏剧中扮演了重要角色。

In December 1986, a meeting of environmentalists was held in Banjarmasin. The meeting was sponsored by the Indonesian network for forests, SKEPHI, an issue-oriented network affiliated with the environmentalist umbrella group WALHI. Both SKEPHI and WALHI imagined themselves at that time as national coalitions of regional grassroots groups; this meeting—SKEPHI’s first national meeting in the provinces—was a demonstration of and an “exercise” in that conception. A provincial nature lovers’ group, Kompas Borneo, hosted the meeting, which involved activists and journalists from around the nation and abroad. Kompas Borneo further demonstrated their grassroots commitment by bringing a local environmental issue to the meeting: the conflict between the inhabitants of the village of Manggur and a timber company cutting trees on the village’s traditional lands. Kompas Borneo brought a group of Manggur men to the meeting to speak, and some seventy-five meeting participants followed these men back to stay in Manggur for several days. SKEPHI and WALHI members also met with employees of the timber company, the Fast Forest Development Company; they spoke, too, with regional officials. As a result of the publicity surrounding these activities, the regional government decided not to renew rights to work the timber concession in that area. The forests returned to Meratus Dayak management. Furthermore, the newly won acclaim of the provincial group, Kompas Borneo, allowed them to garner a Ford Foundation grant to support research in the village; meanwhile, the Jakarta groups SKEPHI and WALHI moved into their strongest periods of forest and forest people’s advocacy.

1986年12月，一场环保主义者会议在班贾尔马辛举行。会议由印尼森林网络 SKEPHI 主办，这是一个以议题为导向的网络，隶属于环保伞状组织 WALHI。当时 SKEPHI 和 WALHI 都把自己想象为地区基层团体的全国联盟；这次会议——SKEPHI 首次在外省举行的全国会议——是对这一构想的一次展示和“演练”。一个省级自然爱好者团体 Kompas Borneo 主办了会议，来自全国和外国的活动家和记者参加了会议。Kompas Borneo 通过把一个当地环境问题带到会议上，进一步展示了他们的基层承诺：芒古尔村居民与一家在村庄传统土地上砍树的木材公司之间的冲突。Kompas Borneo 带了一群芒古尔男子到会上发言，约75名与会者跟随这些人回到芒古尔，在那里逗留数日。SKEPHI 和 WALHI 成员还会见了木材公司快速森林开发公司的雇员；他们也与地区官员交谈。由于这些活动引发的宣传，地区政府决定不再续批该地区伐木特许区的经营权。森林回到梅拉图斯达雅克人的管理中。此外，省级团体 Kompas Borneo 新赢得的声誉使他们获得福特基金会资助，支持在村中的研究；与此同时，雅加达团体 SKEPHI 和 WALHI 进入了其森林与森林人民倡导的最强时期。

This was an environmentalist success. Not only was corporate deforestation halted, at least temporarily, but the process was the one radical Indonesian environmentalists most desired: A village movement enlisted the help of provincial and national activists to win rights to community forest management. Yet the closer one looks, the more confusing the story becomes.
这是一次环保主义的成功。不仅公司的森林砍伐至少暂时停止，而且这一过程正是激进印尼环保主义者最渴望的：一场村庄运动争取到省级和全国活动家的帮助，赢得社群森林管理的权利。然而，越仔细看，故事就越令人困惑。

While I was in the Meratus Mountains in 1986, I was not researching this issue, and I did not attend these meetings. It was only in 1994 that I decided to find out what happened in Manggur. I went to Manggur and spoke to various community leaders and residents. In the provincial capital, Banjarmasin, I spoke to members of Kompas Borneo who had been active in both the original exercise and the ensuing research project. I also spoke to SKEPHI and WALHI members in Jakarta who had participated in the exercise.
1986年我在梅拉图斯山脉时并未研究这个问题，也没有参加这些会议。直到1994年，我才决定弄清芒古尔发生了什么。我去芒古尔，与多位社群领袖和居民交谈。在省会班贾尔马辛，我与 Kompas Borneo 成员交谈，他们既活跃于最初的演练，也活跃于随后的研究项目。我还与雅加达参与演练的 SKEPHI 和 WALHI 成员交谈。

Everyone had a different story. The stories differed in both fact and interpretation. Who were the actors? What happened? My common-sense expectation that the versions would eventually aggregate into a neat composite tripped up against variations in how the space, time, motivation, and process of events were told. I became fascinated by the success of an alliance based on rather complete incomprehensions of collaborators’ points of view.
每个人都有一个不同的故事。这些故事在事实和解释上都不同。行动者是谁？发生了什么？我常识性的期待是这些版本最终会聚合成一幅整齐的合成图，却遭遇了关于事件空间、时间、动机和过程的叙述差异。我开始着迷于一个基于合作者观点相当彻底的不理解而取得成功的联盟。

Had I participated in the events myself, I might have such a clear opinion of what happened that I would only assess the stories I heard in relation to my version of the facts. I might have a good story to tell, but it would be a different story. Here I use the advantage of my absence: All versions seem plausible to me. For my purposes here, I have no need to worry through the question of the “real truth” of what happened in Manggur. Instead, I focus on the enigma of incompatible versions. How can it be that close collaborators have such different stories? This question brings us into the frictions of collaboration.
如果我亲自参与了事件，我可能会有如此明确的看法，以至于只能参照我的事实版本来评价听到的故事。我可能有一个好故事可讲，但会是另一个故事。在这里，我利用自己缺席的优势：所有版本在我看来都可信。就我此处的目的而言，我无需费心追问芒古尔事件的“真实真相”。相反，我聚焦于不相容版本的谜题。密切的合作者怎么会有如此不同的故事？这个问题把我们带入协作的摩擦。

The stories I heard in Manggur, Banjarmasin, and Jakarta are not just varied spins on the same facts; they offer different facts. How did these accounts enter the same universe of conversation? Another story produced them as interlocutors. This is the discursive field that calls these events a grassroots environmental alliance. This discourse offered the speakers a framework for political process; it brought them into conversation and established the basis for both agreement and misunderstanding. The next part of this chapter examines the “grassroots alliance” narrative in Indonesian environmentalism to look at how it produces divergent social locations and sets them in hierarchy. Only then can I return to the divergent perspectives of each group, which go farther than what might be predictable from this hierarchy. As I have established in the previous chapters, village elder, nature lover, and national activist perspectives are produced within different and somewhat autonomously formed understandings of nature. The stories I heard in Manggur, Banjarmasin, and Jakarta spoke differently of the nature of the Meratus forest and of the role of humans in shaping its history. By reviewing these divergent perspectives through their narratives of this event, I suggest how the community-managed forest emerged in their awkward coalescence. The collaborations also produced a new kind of provincial citizen, the “environmentalist,” a nonprofessional expert who is neither quite scientist nor quite politician. The nature we know is produced in such power-laden but unpredictable collaborations.

我在芒古尔、班贾尔马辛和雅加达听到的故事，不只是对同一事实的不同诠释；它们提供不同的事实。这些叙述如何进入同一个对话宇宙？是另一个故事把它们生产为对话者。这是一个把这些事件称为基层环保联盟的话语场域。这一话语为说话者提供了政治过程的框架；它把他们带入对话，为一致和误解同时奠定基础。本章下一部分考察印尼环保主义中的“基层联盟”叙事，看看它如何生产不同的社会位置，并把它们置于等级之中。只有到那时，我才能回到每一组的分歧视角，这些视角比从这一等级中可能预见的走得更远。正如我在前几章所确立的，村庄长者、自然爱好者和全国活动家的视角，是在不同且某种程度上自主形成的自然理解中产生的。我在芒古尔、班贾尔马辛和雅加达听到的故事，对梅拉图斯森林的性质以及人类在塑造其历史中的作用说法不同。通过它们关于这一事件的叙述来回顾这些分歧视角，我提出社群管理的森林如何在它们别扭的汇合中出现。这些协作还生产出一种新型的省级公民——“环保主义者”，一个既不完全像科学家也不完全像政治家的非专业专家。我们所知道的自然，正是在这种充满权力却不可预测的协作中生产出来的。
The Grassroots Alliance and the Production of the Village
基层联盟与村庄的生产

The social subjects of environmentalism are as collaboratively formed as the natural objects. Consider the contrast between agendas that posit humans in nature as indigenous tribes, or as aggregate masses, or as alert villages. The tribes are the ones who are part of nature, wild and innocent as other fauna. And while this is the easiest environmentalism to make fun of, the much more powerful and dangerous mainstream agenda portrays humans as amassed atoms whose sheer density and undifferentiated drive to consumption destroys everything around them. This is the environmentalism that would limit reproduction and cordon off pure nature reserves, or in its equally scary developmentalist versions, empower southern elites in a fantasy of raising everyone’s standard of sustainable living. It is in contrast to these agendas that environmentalists interested in democratic process have imagined the grassroots alliance as a structure that links policy-savvy activists and the rural or urban communities that know the most about their own environmental problems. In this frame, the village is the locus of rural environmental management. When villagers raise their voices about local environmental problems, their environmentalist allies can turn these problems into policy debates and transformations.

环保主义的社会主体与自然对象一样，是协作形成的。想想这些议程之间的对比：它们把自然中的人设定为原住民部落、聚合的群众，或警觉的村庄。部落是自然的一部分，像其他动物一样野性而纯真。虽然这是最容易取笑的环保主义，但更为强大和危险的主流议程把人描绘成积聚的原子，其纯粹密度和无差别的消费驱力摧毁周围一切。这种环保主义会限制生育，圈出纯自然保留地；或者在其同样可怕的发展主义版本中，怀着提高所有人可持续生活水平的幻想，赋权南方精英。正是在与这些议程的对比中，关心民主过程的环保主义者把基层联盟想象为一种结构，连接精通政策的活动家与最了解自身环境问题的乡村或城市社群。在这一框架中，村庄是乡村环境管理的场所。当村民为当地环境问题发声时，他们的环保主义盟友可以把这些问题转化为政策辩论和变革。

In Indonesia, this international environmentalist narrative assumed its particular form in dialogue with the discourse of state authority. During the New Order, Indonesian environmentalists reproduced state hierarchies in the very process of building a populist alternative. The hierarchy meant that Manggur leaders, for example, knew that they could only speak as village spokesmen. Hierarchy was not exterior to their stories, as the image of powerless people speaking back might suggest; power made possible their speaking, even if it did not determine their stories’ content.
在印尼，这种国际环保主义叙事在与国家权威话语的对话中采取了特定形式。新秩序时期，印尼环保主义者在建设民粹主义替代方案的过程中复制了国家等级。这种等级意味着，例如，芒古尔领袖知道自己只能作为村庄发言人说话。等级并非外在于他们的故事，如同无权者回话的形象可能暗示的那样；权力使他们的言说成为可能，即使它并未决定故事的内容。

During the New Order, the hierarchy that structured the differences among village, province, and capital in Indonesia was inscribed so deeply in the architecture of state-connected organizations that it was hard to remember it as a social fact. It appeared as a natural feature of daily life. Yet it was also an imaginative construction, and this is the angle from which we must view it to see its reproduction in the environmental movement.
新秩序时期，建构印尼村庄、省会和首都之间差异的等级，深深铭刻在与国家相连的组织架构中，以至于很难把它记作一项社会事实。它显得像日常生活的自然特征。然而它也是一种想象性建构，我们必须从这个角度观察它，才能看到它在环保运动中的再生产。

A “village” in this discourse is the unit of rural community. Questions of community formation and history do not need to be asked; they are taken for granted. Obviously, one assumes, rural people cohere into villages. By definition, village leaders always speak for the people. Or so it seemed during the New Order.
As soon as the regime fell in 1998, rural leaders all over the country demanded to be counted in units other than villages. In 1986, such defiance seemed unthinkable.
在这一话语中，“村庄”是乡村社群的单位。社群形成与历史的问题无需提出；它们被视作理所当然。显然，人们假定乡村人凝聚为村庄。按定义，村庄领袖总是为人民说话。至少在新秩序时期看起来如此。
1998年政权一倒台，全国各地的乡村领袖就要求以村庄以外的单位被计算。1986年，这种违抗似乎不可想象。

In contrast to the village, the capital was imagined as the site of policy making. National political action “of course” takes place in the capital. (To avoid the homogenizing term “national,” I will use the term “capital” to refer to perspectives from the national capital.) The capital, in this logic, needs no community identity because it is the place where action is planned for communities, that is, other places. During the New Order, no options were apparent. Yet its artificial status emerged clearly once the New Order fell; one of the first projects for transition was the dismantling of this hierarchy through decentralization.
与村庄相对，首都被想象为政策制定的场所。国家的政治行动“当然”发生在首都。（为避免“全国的”这一同质化术语，我将用“首都”指来自国家首都的视角。）按这种逻辑，首都无需社群身份，因为它是为社群——即其他地方——规划行动的地方。新秩序时期，看不到其他选项。然而一旦新秩序倒台，其人为状态就清楚显现；转型的最初项目之一就是通过分权拆除这一等级。

Finally, the provincial capital was designed as the site where the planning from the national capital is put into practice. (To differentiate these, I will use “provincial” alone to refer to the provincial capital.) Awkwardly, it was to be both agent and regional adviser of the capital; its institutional distinctiveness rested on this awkwardness. Post-New Order political thinkers are confused, indeed, about what to do with the province: Should it be a unit of regional autonomy or of national centralization, or should it be quietly dismantled?
最后，省会被设计为把首都规划付诸实践的场所。（为区分两者，我将单用“省”来指省会。）别扭的是，它既要当首都的代理人，又要当向首都提供地区事务建议的顾问；其制度独特性正建立在这种别扭之上。新秩序后的政治思想家确实困惑于如何处理省级层面：它应是地区自治的单位，还是国家集权的单位，或者应被悄然拆除？

Movements for political reform were very much limited during the New Order. Only those political parties organized by the state were approved, and even they were allowed to speak only just before elections. Workers’ movements, religious movements, and regional rights movements were actively repressed. Environmentalism squeaked by at the edge of legitimacy in part because movement leaders were willing to maintain a respectful dialogue with the state. In this context, it is not surprising that environmentalism reproduced certain categories of New Order political culture—even as they challenged state policies.
新秩序时期，政治改革运动受到很大限制。只有国家组织的政党得到批准，即使它们也只被允许在选举前发言。工人运动、宗教运动和地区权利运动遭到积极压制。环保主义在合法性的边缘勉强通过，部分因为运动领袖愿意与国家保持尊重的对话。在这种背景下，环保主义复制新秩序政治文化的某些范畴并不奇怪——即使它们在挑战国家政策。

The necessity of presenting itself as nonpolitical shaped the politics of the emerging environmental movement as it coalesced in Jakarta in the 1980s. The nature imagined by WALHI has always been populated, defined, and managed by people. Yet it was never possible to cast environmentalism as a form of political mobilization. Environmentalists might protect the forms of nature and natural management that already exist; but they ought not be creating political desires. The Indonesian Communist Party had mobilized across the country in the 1960s, and they had gotten killed for it. Environmentalists could see themselves as advocates for rights and management practices that already existed; but they needed to obscure any consciousness raising that their own efforts created. In this context, an already popular theme of much urban intellectual culture blossomed: the division between the wealth and alienation of urban elites, on the one hand, and the poverty, communal sociality, and wisdom of rural villagers, on the other. Jakarta environmentalists working on rural issues began to see their role as the protection of already existing rural wisdom.

在20世纪80年代于雅加达汇合时，新兴环保运动必须把自己呈现为非政治性的，这塑造了它的政治。WALHI 所想象的自然一直是由人居住、界定和管理的。然而把环保主义塑造成一种政治动员形式从来不可能。环保主义者可以保护已经存在的自然形式与自然管理形式；但他们不应创造政治欲望。印尼共产党曾在20世纪60年代在全国动员，并因此遭到屠杀。环保主义者可以把自己视为对已有权利与管理实践的倡导者；但他们需要掩盖自身努力所创造的任何意识提升。在这种背景下，许多城市知识分子文化中一个本已流行的主题开花：一边是城市精英的财富与异化，另一边是乡村村民的贫困、社群社会性与智慧。处理乡村问题的雅加达环保主义者开始把自己的角色视为保护已经存在的乡村智慧。

This agenda was in many ways a critique of the government's development program. New Order development treated villages as units of collective ignorance to be brought up to development’s progress-oriented standards. In contrast, the capital’s environmentalists argued that village people have better schemes of resource management than the government. New Order development used provincial offices to execute national orders; in contrast, the capital’s environmentalists invited provincial groups to raise issues. But in the classic fashion of a counter-discourse, the government's administrative hierarchy was reproduced in these reversals. Villages remained the natural units of rural community. The capital remained the site of policy decisions. The provinces remained the site of regional mediation between policies and people. Indeed, the naturalization of this division of roles has been a major subject of progressive self-examination in the post-New Order era.

这一议程在许多方面是对政府发展计划的批评。新秩序发展把村庄视为集体无知的单位，需要被提升到发展以进步为导向的标准。相比之下，首都的环保主义者论证说，村庄人民拥有比政府更好的资源管理方案。新秩序发展利用省级办公室执行国家命令；相比之下，首都的环保主义者邀请省级团体提出问题。但按照反话语的经典方式，政府的行政等级在这些颠倒中被复制。村庄仍然是乡村社群的天然单位。首都仍然是政策决定的场所。省仍然是政策与人民之间的地区中介场所。确实，这种角色分工的自然化，一直是新秩序后进步派自我审视的主要主题。

During the New Order, however, the three-tiered hierarchy became institutionalized in WALHI precisely as a piece of its most populist anti-state stance. WALHI is an umbrella group, the focus point of a network, and not a monolithic management agency. Key to its functioning has been the Regional Forum in each province; provincial groups are to raise the issues that inform WALHI’s central organizers. The Regional Forum should have contacts in the villages, which thus are the ultimate site of agenda setting. You can see the appeal of this democratic process for the provinces and villages: The provinces are to raise issues, not just carry out policy; village leaders are to speak for the people, not just obey orders. Working together, then, spokespeople from these different levels, with a new sense of empowerment, reproduced a hierarchy that defined their structural distinctions, forming both limitations and creative possibilities.

然而在新秩序时期，这种三层等级恰恰作为 WALHI 最民粹主义的反国家立场的一部分，在 WALHI 内部制度化了。WALHI 是一个伞状团体，一个网络的焦点，而不是铁板一块的管理机构。其运作的关键是各省的地区论坛；省级团体提出问题，为 WALHI 中央组织者提供信息。地区论坛应在村庄有联系人，村庄因此是议程设定的最终场所。你可以看到这种民主过程对省和村庄的吸引力：省要提出问题，而不只是执行政策；村庄领袖要为人民说话，而不只是服从命令。于是，来自这些不同层级的发言人带着新的赋权感共同工作，复制了一个界定其结构性差异的等级，既形成限制，也形成创造性的可能。

The activists I spoke to in Manggur, Banjarmasin, and Jakarta spoke from their roles as village leaders, provincial advocates, and capital organizers, respectively: Village leaders spoke of community rights; provincial advocates spoke of raising issues; capital organizers spoke of building policy. These roles, however, did not determine their definitions of environmental problems and of the forms of political agency that could address them. In the next sections, I propose that activists in these different locations told different stories because they had developed contrasting histories of the Manggur forest. These histories did not complement each other within the national hierarchy I have described; instead they challenged each other, and thus formed the grounds for unexpected overlaps and dialogues.

我在芒古尔、班贾尔马辛和雅加达交谈的活动家，分别从村庄领袖、省级倡导者和首都组织者的角色说话：村庄领袖谈论社群权利；省级倡导者谈论提出问题；首都组织者谈论建设政策。然而这些角色并未决定他们对环境问题的定义，也未决定他们眼中能够应对这些问题的政治能动性形式。在接下来的几节中，我提出这些不同地点的活动家讲述不同故事，是因为他们发展出了关于芒古尔森林的对比性历史。这些历史并未在我所描述的全国等级中相互补充；相反，它们相互挑战，从而为意外的重叠与对话奠定了基础。
Forest History 1: Recording at the Edge of the Wild
森林史一：在荒野边缘记录

I begin with the province, since it was here that, as was appropriate in the political hierarchy, the issue of Manggur was raised for a wider audience. Kompas Borneo was formed in the late 1970s by students at the provincial university. The group organized adventures in nature, particularly hikes in the forests of the Meratus Mountains. A first-person account can offer the flavor of Kompas Borneo’s growing involvement with Meratus Dayaks in the 1980s:

Sometime in the 1970s a helicopter of the Conoco oil company crashed into a Meratus mountainside. We heard about it in an article in Tempo about savage murders. [Until state censors shut it down in 1994, Tempo was the country’s leading news magazine.] The article said that the local Dayaks cut the body of the American pilot in half. We decided to go look for the remnants of the helicopter. It took us several trips; at first, the Dayaks were suspicious of us and sent us in the wrong direction. Finally, after several expeditions, they got to know us, and a Dayak man accepted us as adopted children. They took us to the place where some rusted scraps still remain.
我从省开始，因为正是在这里，按照政治等级的应有方式，芒古尔问题被提给更广泛的受众。Kompas Borneo 由省立大学的学生于20世纪70年代末创立。这个团体组织自然探险，尤其是在梅拉图斯山脉森林中徒步。一段第一人称叙述可以让人感受 Kompas Borneo 在20世纪80年代与梅拉图斯达雅克人日益加深的接触：

1970年代的某个时候，Conoco 石油公司的一架直升机坠毁在梅拉图斯山坡上。我们在《Tempo》杂志一篇关于野蛮谋杀的文章中得知此事。〔1994年被国家审查机构关闭之前，《Tempo》是该国首屈一指的新闻杂志。〕文章说，当地达雅克人把美国飞行员的尸体砍成两半。我们决定去寻找直升机残骸。我们去了好几次；起初，达雅克人不信任我们，把我们指向错误方向。最后，经过几次探险，他们认识了我们，一位达雅克男子认我们作自己的孩子。他们带我们去了那个仍留有锈蚀碎片的地方。

We began to go back to these villages as our hiking destinations, and we became interested in their social and cultural life. One of the villages was Manggur. There, we heard about their problems with Fast Forest Development Company, which had begun timbering operations in the area. The timber concession went right across village land. Besides, it was located in an area that had been zoned as a watershed-protection forest since the colonial era. We were looking for an issue then, and so we decided to raise the issue of Manggur. When the WALHI summit meeting was held in Banjarmasin, we brought down several Manggur leaders so they could explain the problem directly to the meeting. We then took the participants on a field trip to Manggur for three days. Journalists were there from all over the ASEAN region. The regent in that sector was afraid that he had a “Bruno Manser problem” on his hands, and so he refused to sign the papers renewing the timber company’s right to work there.

我们开始把这些村庄当作徒步目的地，并对它们的社会文化生活产生兴趣。其中一个村庄就是芒古尔。在那里，我们听说他们与快速森林开发公司的问题，该公司已开始在该地区伐木。伐木特许区正好横跨村庄土地。此外，它位于自殖民时代起就被划为水源保护林的地区。当时我们正在寻找一个议题，于是决定提出芒古尔问题。当 WALHI 峰会在班贾尔马辛举行时，我们带了几位芒古尔领袖下山，让他们直接向会议解释问题。然后我们带与会者到芒古尔实地考察三天。来自东盟各地的记者在那里。该地区的县长担心自己手上有一个“布鲁诺·曼瑟问题”，因此拒绝签署续批木材公司开采权的文件。

Bruno Manser was the Swiss nature lover who made an international cause of the destruction of the forests inhabited by the Penan of Sarawak, East Malaysia. Like Manser, Kompas Borneo members saw themselves as different kinds of people than the indigenous Borneans they pledged to protect. They were able to speak for Dayaks because, unlike Dayaks, they themselves were not isolated primitives who chopped up alien helicopter pilots, but, instead, cosmopolitan citizens. It is in this framework that rainforest adventures can become social causes. Civilized people who reach out to touch the wild can speak for it at the edge of its destruction. As history comes in to threaten traditional communities and the forests they husband, environmentalists speak as critical witnesses.

The ability to speak both about and for Dayaks and their forests defined what it came to mean to be an “environmentalist” in Banjarmasin. The members of Kompas Borneo began as nature lovers but became more and more interested in environmental advocacy causes. Still, they were not, for the most part, professional activists or ecologists. When the group wrote their successful grant proposal for continuing research in Manggur (LSPMKB 1987), they identified themselves mainly through the English term “environmentalist,” despite the fact that most had other jobs—as law professors, journalists, or the like. Through their role in raising the issue of Manggur, they became experts, not by disciplinary training but by their unique positioning. They became environmentalists as advocates for nature and the people who live in it; they could stand at the edge of the wild to record and preserve it. They spoke for the people and their forests—but they were not fully of them.

布鲁诺·曼瑟是一位瑞士自然爱好者，他把东马沙捞越本南人居住的森林遭到破坏变成了一项国际事业。像曼瑟一样，Kompas Borneo 成员把自己看作与他们承诺保护的原住民婆罗洲人不同的人。他们能够为达雅克人说话，是因为与达雅克人不同，他们自己不是砍碎外来的直升机飞行员的孤立原始人，而是世界主义公民。正是在这一框架中，雨林探险可以变成社会事业。伸手触摸荒野的文明人，可以在荒野毁灭的边缘为它发声。当历史前来威胁传统社群及其照管的森林时，环保主义者作为批判性见证者发言。

既能谈论达雅克人及其森林，又能为他们说话的能力，界定了在班贾尔马辛成为“环保主义者”意味着什么。Kompas Borneo 成员起初是自然爱好者，但越来越关注环保倡导事业。不过，他们大多不是专业活动家或生态学家。当这个团体撰写后来获批的、用于继续在芒古尔开展研究的资助申请（LSPMKB 1987）时，他们主要通过英语术语“environmentalist”来表明自己的身份，尽管大多数人另有工作——如法学教授、记者等。通过他们在提出芒古尔问题中的角色，他们成为专家，不是靠学科训练，而是靠独特的定位。他们成为环保主义者，作为自然及生活在其中的人的倡导者；他们可以站在荒野边缘记录并保存它。他们为人民及其森林说话——但他们并不完全属于其中。

How was this positioning accomplished? I’m interested here in the ways in which stories engage with and create the materiality of the world. The most developed version of Kompas Borneo’s environmentalism is found in the series of documents they wrote about Manggur for the Ford Foundation, the provincial government, and the newspaper, between 1987 and 1991.

The most surprising thing about these documents to me was the fact that the role of Manggur people as agents in a struggle against the Fast Forest Development Company completely disappeared. Manggur became a traditional community about to enter history for the first time.
这种定位是如何完成的？我感兴趣的是故事介入并创造世界物质性的方式。Kompas Borneo 环保主义最成熟的版本，见于他们1987年至1991年间为福特基金会、省政府和报纸撰写的关于芒古尔的一系列文件。
这些文件最令我惊讶的是，芒古尔人作为反抗快速森林开发公司斗争中的行动者角色完全消失了。芒古尔变成了一个即将首次进入历史的传统社群。

In the 1987 grant proposal, for example, Manggur is presented as a typical Dayak community poised uncertainly at the edge of modernity (LSPMKB 1987). On one side, the Fast Forest Development Company threatens to bring too much development too fast. On the other side, a proposed nature reserve requires standards of conservation that are incompatible with human habitation. This is modernity, with its segregation of culture and nature. The traditional Meratus of Manggur are caught in the middle, still outside of history, but vulnerable and confused.
例如，在1987年的资助申请中，芒古尔被呈现为一个典型的达雅克社群，不确定地停留在现代性的边缘（LSPMKB 1987）。一方面，快速森林开发公司威胁带来过多过快的发展。另一方面，一个拟议的自然保护区要求与人类居住不相容的保护标准。这就是现代性，带着它对文化与自然的隔离。芒古尔的传统梅拉图斯人被夹在中间，仍在历史之外，却脆弱而困惑。

The proposal waffles about the relationship between Manggur and the forest. It praises Manggur’s traditional forest management for maintaining the forest. Yet it argues that local livelihood practices will destroy the natural surroundings if development assistance is not forthcoming. Tradition saves nature; tradition destroys nature: The proposal tells it both ways, combining rhetorics of development, conservation, and cultural survival. In one telling fragment, the group suggests that they build model houses for Manggur villagers to help them develop. Later, they say that the houses will be built in the local style. This cannot but raise the question: What is wrong with the houses they already have?
申请书在芒古尔与森林的关系上摇摆不定。它赞扬芒古尔传统森林管理维护了森林。然而它又论证说，如果发展援助不到位，当地生计实践将破坏自然环境。传统拯救自然；传统毁灭自然：申请书两种说法都讲，混合了发展、保护和文化生存的修辞。在一个说明性的片段中，该团体建议为芒古尔村民建造示范房屋，帮助他们发展。后来又说是按照当地风格建造。这不禁让人发问：他们现有的房屋有什么问题？

Manggur is presented both as a community living in harmony with nature, whose traditions should be recorded and preserved, and as a community that must be improved in order to use and conserve nature more appropriately. The role of the expert is double: to record, advocate, and revere, on the one hand, and to guide, manage, and modify, on the other. This was a challenging agenda in the authoritarian development climate of the provinces. I do not mean to slight the enormous courage and intelligence of its advocates by focusing on its contradictions. Yet these contradictions are important in examining cultural gaps and linkages. I suggest that these contradictions have been held in place, with difficulty, precisely by the moment of alliance. It is only through Kompas Borneo’s collaboration with SKEPHI and WALHI, on the one hand, and with Manggur leaders, on the other, that they were able to maintain for themselves the tension of their joint role as advocate-guides and researcher-developers, that is, provincial environmentalists. In the next sections I show that the way these collaborations work to stabilize this position of expertise reverses our expectations. It is the collaboration with capital organizers that stabilizes provincial expectations of the community that should be preserved—the wise community that lives with and manages nature. The collaboration with village leaders stabilizes involvement with the government's policy hierarchy, with its rhetoric of development, which can give community advocates the strength to survive.

芒古尔既被呈现为一个与自然和谐共处、其传统应被记录和保存的社群，又被呈现为一个必须被改进、以便更恰当地利用和保护自然的社群。专家的角色是双重的：一方面记录、倡导和崇敬，另一方面引导、管理和改造。在各省专制的发展气候中，这是一项具有挑战性的议程。我无意通过聚焦其矛盾来轻视倡导者巨大的勇气和智慧。然而这些矛盾对考察文化鸿沟与连接很重要。我认为，这些矛盾正是被联盟的时刻艰难地固定住的。只有通过 Kompas Borneo 一方面与 SKEPHI 和 WALHI、另一方面与芒古尔领袖的协作，他们才能为自己维持其作为倡导—引导者与研究者—开发者的双重角色的张力，也就是省级环保主义者的张力。在接下来的几节中，我将说明这些协作稳定这一专家位置的方式如何反转我们的期待。正是与首都组织者的协作，稳定了省对应当被保存的社群的期待——那个与自然共处并管理自然的智慧社群。与村庄领袖的协作，则稳定了与政府政策等级及其发展修辞的牵连，而这种修辞可以给社群倡导者生存下去的力量。
Forest History 2: Managing the People’s Gardens
森林史二：管理人民的园圃

I turn briefly to the view from the capital. Briefly, because no one in Jakarta cared much about what happened in Manggur. The event was an exercise, a textbook problem that helped to establish a paradigm. Its details were unimportant in themselves. The organizer mainly remembered the problems of running a conference: making sure the arrangements are in place, worrying about the food preparation. She remembered that Manggur was a beautiful place, and that the village people were friendly. She remembered arranging meetings with the timber company management and with the regency and provincial government; she advocated a chain of negotiations, rather than any single confrontation, as the most effective strategy. Like other Jakarta participants, she had not followed up on the case and was unaware that the timber company had been turned away from that sector of its concession. Successes such as that are rare, she added, asking me to write up a version of the events to remind WALHI activists that grassroots advocacy can work (Tsing 1995).

我简要转向首都的视角。之所以简要，是因为雅加达没有人太关心芒古尔发生了什么。这次事件是一次演练，一个帮助确立范式的教科书问题。其细节本身并不重要。组织者主要记得办会议的麻烦：确保安排到位，担心食物准备。她记得芒古尔是个美丽的地方，村民很友好。她记得安排与木材公司管理层以及县和省政府会面；她主张一连串谈判，而不是任何单一对抗，作为最有效的策略。像其他雅加达参与者一样，她没有跟进此案，也不知道木材公司已被赶出特许区的那个地段。这样的成功很罕见，她补充说，并请我写一个事件版本，提醒 WALHI 活动家基层倡导可以奏效（Tsing 1995）。

The details of what happened in Manggur were less important in the capital than the model of forest history that Manggur helped to build for both WALHI and SKEPHI. In this model, forests are not wild places—as they were for Kompas Borneo; they are populated and managed, not by wild, primitive people but by familiar social communities. The history of forests involves not the modernization of the wild, but the struggle between resource-greedy institutions, such as the colonial and national state and the logging companies they authorize, and local communities of forest-dwelling peoples. Forest-dwelling peoples manage their environments through customary rules and practices. Deforestation is caused not, as the developers claim, by village ignorance and consumption but rather by commercial logging ventures and authoritarian resource control, which wrest the landscape away from village management. Environmentalism is populist advocacy because it is the support network for the grassroots struggle of communities for their long-established land and resource rights.

在首都，芒古尔发生什么的细节，不如芒古尔帮助 WALHI 和 SKEPHI 建立的森林史模型重要。在这个模型中，森林不是荒野——不像对 Kompas Borneo 那样；它们由熟悉的社会社群居住和管理，而不是由野性原始人居住和管理。森林的历史不涉及荒野的现代化，而涉及贪求资源的制度——如殖民国家和民族国家及其授权的伐木公司——与森林居民的地方社群之间的斗争。森林居民通过习惯规则和实践管理环境。森林砍伐的原因不是发展工作者所称的村庄无知和消费，而是商业伐木经营活动和专制资源控制，它们把地景从村庄管理中夺走。环保主义是民粹主义倡导，因为它是社群为长期存在的土地和资源权利进行基层斗争的支持网络。

I myself like this populist narrative, which has numerous advantages over more powerful alternative forest histories. It may be the best tool we have to convince governments and international agencies that there are alternatives to handing the forests to logging companies. In describing it as a narrative, I do not mean to be unsympathetic to its claims, but rather to point to their specificity. In particular, it is important to notice that this is not a history told, like that of Kompas Borneo, at the edge of the wild.
我自己喜欢这种民粹主义叙事，它比更强大的替代性森林史有许多优势。它也许是我们拥有的最好工具，用以说服政府和国际机构：除了把森林交给伐木公司，还有别的选择。把它描述为一种叙事，我并非对其主张缺乏同情，而是要指出其特殊性。尤其重要的是注意到，这不是像 Kompas Borneo 那样在荒野边缘讲述的历史。

How is it, then, that WALHI and SKEPHI were able to work with Kompas Borneo, despite their divergent understandings of the agency of the forest and its people? What they shared was the idea that Manggur was a community—a traditional, coherent, well-organized consensus of people who lived relatively stably with the forest. The kinds of community they imagined were different: The capital’s village was a management unit, long engaged in histories of struggle against greedy outsiders; the province’s village was a cultural unit, as yet unaware of the alienating but civilizing effects of history and struggle. In other words, in the province, history had only just begun for Manggur; the capital supported one moment in a continuous social history. Moreover, the capital’s village community was united by rational resource planning; the province’s village community was united by traditional ritual. But these two notions of community had enough in common to form the basis of an alliance—an alliance to let the villagers of a place such as Manggur speak. Both provincial and capital activists worked to protect the Manggur community and the forest that was central, in both views, to defining community. The Manggur drama depended on this overlap of understandings. And the subsequent strength of environmentalism in both the province and the capital drew from it.

那么，尽管 WALHI 和 SKEPHI 与 Kompas Borneo 对森林及其居民能动性的理解不同，它们为何仍能相互合作？他们共享的观念是：芒古尔是一个社群——一群与森林相对稳定地共处、具有传统、凝聚力和良好组织、达成共识的人。他们想象的社群种类不同：首都的村庄是一个管理单位，长期从事反抗贪婪外来者的斗争史；省的村庄是一个文化单位，尚未意识到历史与斗争的异化却文明化的效果。换句话说，在省里，芒古尔的历史才刚刚开始；首都则支持一段连续社会史中的某个时刻。此外，首都的村庄社群由理性的资源规划团结起来；省的村庄社群由传统仪式团结起来。但这两种社群概念有足够的共同点，构成联盟的基础——一个让芒古尔之类地方的村民说话的联盟。省级和首都活动家都致力于保护芒古尔社群以及在这两种观点中都是界定社群核心的森林。芒古尔戏剧依赖于这种理解的叠合。省和首都随后环保主义的力量都从中汲取。
Forest History 3: Trees Are Social Networks
森林史三：树木是社会网络

Ironically, the coherence of community has been no simple matter in Manggur. Since 1982, Manggur has been the name of a village, that is, a government administrative unit, as well as the politically central settlement location in this unit. Before this reorganization, this location was part of a much wider “village” area, and not its politically central settlement. Both before and after reorganization, the groups and settlements of the area have moved around and regrouped. Here, most families maintain a residence in a jointly constructed and maintained hall, the balai; they also have another house on their swidden field. Balai halls are rebuilt every few years, and particularly at that point families split off with other groups, come into the group, or move the balai to another location. New swidden fields are made every year, and their shifting locations influence and are influenced by a family’s changing direction of social ties. When I visited the area in 1980, many of the 1994 residents of Manggur were living in a balai site called Purun, which by 1994 no longer existed as a settlement site or a social group. In this context, in which there is little to stop individuals and families from continually reshuffling their social ties and geographical locations, pulling together a “community”—and keeping it together—is an ongoing challenge.

讽刺的是，社群的连贯性在芒古尔从来不是简单的事。自1982年以来，芒古尔一直是一个村庄——即政府行政单位——的名称，也是该单位在政治上中心的定居点。重组之前，这个地点属于一个更广阔的“村庄”区域，而不是其政治中心定居点。重组前后，该地区的群体和定居点都曾移动和重组。在这里，大多数家庭在一座共同建造和维护的会堂——balai——中保有住所；他们在游耕地上还有另一座房子。Balai 会堂每隔几年重建，尤其在那时，家庭会同其他群体一起分离出去、加入群体，或把 balai 移到另一地点。每年开辟新的游耕地，其移动位置影响并受家庭社会关系变化方向的影响。1980年我访问该地区时，1994年芒古尔的许多居民住在一个叫普伦的 balai 地点，到1994年，那里已不再是定居点或社会群体。在这种几乎没有什么能阻止个人和家庭不断重新洗牌其社会关系和地理位置的背景下，聚合成一个“社群”——并保持其聚合——是一项持续的挑战。

The landscape plays a major role in community building—as well as community dispersing—in the Meratus Mountains. As I discussed in chapter 5, groves of fruit trees, some carefully planted and some sprouting from discarded seeds, develop around settlement sites; even when people move away, these groves remain as markers of a community that may re-form in the future on the basis of its ongoing, tree-made memories. Most people maintain allegiances not only to the groves and neighbors of their current locations but also to older groves and past neighbors, with whom they may live again. Similarly, the vegetation that grows up as a rice swidden returns to forest makes this secondary forest not just a site of memory but also of ongoing use for those who tended the spot. Some of this vegetation is planted, some encouraged, some cleaned and managed, some mainly ignored. It draws its human associates back again and again into the social community of those who have farmed or tended or foraged contiguous and overlapping locations. Furthermore, many individual trees in the forest, including fruit trees, starch palms, rattans, and the forest emergents on which honey bees build their nests, are claimed. Claimed trees pass to the descendents of claimants; they draw siblings and cousins through their common claims. Collective harvests of fruits, honey, and starch, in contrast, gather friends and neighbors who may or may not be kin, and who come to the base of the tree following the tree claimants who announce the harvest. These trees, and the charismatic individuals who draw harvesters to their bases, become social as well as geographic focal points in group formation. The history of the Meratus forest is a history of social networking. The forested landscape is not just managed by social networks or a model for them; it is simultaneously the shaper of social networks and the material through which they are shaped.

地景在梅拉图斯山脉的社群建设——以及社群分散——中发挥主要作用。正如我在第五章所讨论的，定居点周围会形成果树林，有些是精心栽种的，有些从丢弃的种子发芽；即使人们搬走，这些树林仍作为社群的标记留存下来，社群可能基于其持续的、由树木制造的记忆在未来重新形成。大多数人不仅忠于当前地点的树林和邻居，也忠于更早的树林和过去的邻居，他们可能再次与其共同生活。同样，稻作游耕地恢复为森林时长出的植被，使这片次生林不仅是记忆之地，也是照料此地者持续利用之地。这些植被有些是栽种的，有些是被鼓励生长的，有些被清理和管理，有些主要被忽视。它一次又一次地把其人类伙伴拉回社会社群，这些人曾耕种、照料或采集相邻而重叠的地点。此外，森林中许多单株树木，包括果树、淀粉棕榈、藤和蜜蜂筑巢的突出于林冠的树木，都是有认领者的。被认领的树木传给认领者的后代；它们通过共同认领把兄弟姐妹和堂表亲联系起来。相比之下，果实、蜂蜜和淀粉的集体收获，聚集的是可能是也可能不是亲属的朋友和邻居，他们跟随宣布收获的树木认领者来到树下。这些树木，以及把采集者吸引到树下的魅力人物，成为群体形成中社会和地理的焦点。梅拉图斯森林的历史是一部社会网络的历史。森林地景不仅由社会网络管理，或作为其模型；它同时是社会网络的塑造者，也是社会网络得以被塑造的物质。

Meratus social networks do not stop at the edge of the forest. Community leaders forge real and imagined ties with the officials, police, and merchants of surrounding Banjar towns; from the Meratus perspective, these regional authorities grant Meratus leaders the power to lead. Meratus leaders have long learned to submit to and to mimic the rhetoric of regional and state authority as a condition of autonomy—and of convincing local constituencies that they are powerful enough to lead. Their leadership strategies draw boundaries, paths, and shifting centers into the history of the forest. Leaders tell the boundaries of state-recognized, once-recognized, or hoping-to-be-recognized village and neighborhood communities; of course, claims overlap. People’s movements toward and away from markets and centers of regional authority create directional paths. Coexisting social clusters compete for status as a local center, a drawing place for community.

梅拉图斯社会网络并不止于森林边缘。社群领袖与周围班贾尔城镇的官员、警察和商人建立真实和想象的纽带；从梅拉图斯视角看，这些地区权威授予梅拉图斯领袖领导权力。梅拉图斯领袖早已学会服从并模仿地区和国家权威的修辞，作为自治的条件——并说服当地支持者相信自己强大到足以领导。他们的领导策略把边界、路径和移动的中心带入森林历史。领袖讲述得到国家承认、曾经得到承认或希望得到承认的村庄与邻里社群的边界；当然，主张相互重叠。人们向市场和地区权威中心移动或远离，创造出方向性路径。共存的社会集群竞争作为地方中心的地位，即社群的汇聚之地。

Given these shifting flows of community associations, Manggur had done very well in the 1980s. A sibling set of nine adults and their families formed a cohesive core, which in itself was big enough to call “community,” and attracted others besides. One of the older brothers was an ambitious and charismatic man who managed to get appointed to the position of village head in the late 1960s, when the village was still a huge territory. He made good political connections, and in 1994 his words still carried much weight. His history of leadership helps explain how his residence in the early 1980s won the position of central location for the newly recognized smaller village—Manggur. (Not every settlement was so lucky. Four other hamlets, not located in the spot called Manggur, are part of the administrative village.) Meanwhile, one of his younger sisters became village head of the new village in 1982, and she continued to be village head in Manggur through the 1990s. The youngest brother was village secretary. And these three people—whose identities are so continuous with the positing of “Manggur” as a political entity at all—were consistently the main players in the environmentalist drama I have been describing.

鉴于这些社群联合的流动，芒古尔在20世纪80年代做得很好。九位成年兄弟姐妹及各自家庭组成一个凝聚的核心，其本身已大到足以称为“社群”，还吸引了其他人。其中一位较年长的兄弟是一个有野心、有魅力的人，他在20世纪60年代末设法被任命为村长，当时村庄还是一个巨大的领地。他建立了良好的政治关系，到1994年，他的话仍有很大分量。他的领导史有助于解释，他在20世纪80年代初的住所如何赢得新获承认的较小村庄——芒古尔——中心位置的地位。（并非每个定居点都如此幸运。另外四个小村不在称为芒古尔的地点，但属于行政村庄。）与此同时，他的一个妹妹于1982年成为新村的村长，并一直担任芒古尔村长到20世纪90年代。最小的弟弟是村庄秘书。这三个人——他们的身份与“芒古尔”作为一个政治实体的设定如此连续——一直是我所描述的环保戏剧中的主要角色。

With this background material, you may not be surprised to hear that the stories these three individuals told are different from those I heard from SKEPHI and Kompas Borneo. My original anxiety about contradictory versions, however, developed as I heard the village head tell the story: Although she remembered and delighted in telling me about the December 1986 meeting in Manggur, she timed the environmental victory as coming before this event, in 1985. That victory consisted of moving the timber company out of the forest of her social network into the forest of other Meratus social networks. Here is a piece of her story:
有了这些背景材料，你也许不会惊讶于听到，这三个人讲述的故事与我听 SKEPHI 和 Kompas Borneo 讲的不同。然而，我最初始对矛盾版本的焦虑，是在听村长讲述时形成的：尽管她记得并乐于向我讲述1986年12月的芒古尔会议，她把环境胜利的时间定在这次事件之前，即1985年。那场胜利是把木材公司从她社会网络的森林移入其他梅拉图斯社会网络的森林。以下是她的故事片段：

In 1983, the timber company made a road near here. Ten Manggur families moved down to the road. [Moving to the road showed compliance with state civilizational standards, even as it aggravated the company.] The timber company filed an official complaint that we were cutting swiddens in the timber concession. If they had not complained, we would never have gotten involved; they could have kept cutting for ten years. But we were forced to meet with the government. I had to go down to government offices constantly; I barely could stay two nights in a row at home. That was when I was still energetic; I would be tired of it now.
1983年，木材公司在这里附近修了一条路。十个芒古尔家庭搬到路边。〔搬到路边显示了对国家文明标准的服从，即使这激怒了公司。〕木材公司正式投诉我们在伐木特许区内开垦游耕地。如果他们不投诉，我们绝不会卷入；他们本可以继续砍十年。但我们被迫与政府会面。我必须不断去政府办公室；我几乎无法在家连续住两晚。那时我仍精力充沛；现在我会厌倦的。

I went to the District Office and finally even to the office of the governor. I would never have been brave enough to go there except that the company had said we were at fault. The company had blamed us, saying that shifting cultivation caused succession to grassland [hilalang, the tropical grass Imperata cylindrica, which forms forest-excluding grasslands]. I argued back, that there was no proof of this; there is no grassland in Manggur, and there never has been.
我去了区公所，最后甚至去了省长的办公室。要不是公司说我们有错，我绝不敢去那里。公司责备我们，说游耕导致演替为草地〔hilalang，即热带草类白茅（Imperata cylindrica），会形成排挤森林的草地〕。我反驳说，没有证据；芒古尔没有草地，从来也没有。

The governor told me that by chance there was a meeting of Forestry Department officials from the capital there, and I should consult with them. I went to the Forestry official and I said, “Maybe we are at fault, but I would like to see the map of the timber concession.” They had a map that showed that the concession was really located in the next district! They had been stealing logs from our district. The official cancelled the forestry meeting and took me back to the district; within a week the company was turned out. They moved their operations to the next district. After that, everything has been peaceful.
省长告诉我，恰好首都林业部官员在那里开会，我应该咨询他们。我去找林业官员，说：“也许我们有错，但我想看看伐木特许区的地图。”他们有一张地图，显示特许区实际上位于邻区！他们一直在从我们区盗伐木材。这位官员取消了林业会议，带我回区里；一周之内，公司被赶走。他们把业务搬到邻区。此后，一切太平。

My starting assumption is that most of this story is true. The contradictions in timing could be produced by what counts as success: For the village head, it is a consolidation of her village territory; for Kompas Borneo, it is the growing legitimacy of environmental politics regionally; for WALHI, it is the practice of grassroots support against government coercion and corporate land grabs. However, the village head’s story also needs to be considered within genres of Meratus leadership narratives, in which, in my experience, not every meeting between the narrating leader and the external authority that empowers him or her to speak could have physically occurred. Since the power to lead is granted by these ties to powerful outsiders, every leader I knew told of meetings with regional authority, for a community ideally forms around the power of this story. What really happened? This question is more puzzling still in the story I heard from the charismatic and forceful older brother, who, like his sister, put himself in the center of the action, never mentioning the other. Here is a fragment:

我的出发假设是这个故事大部分是真的。时间上的矛盾可能由什么算作成功造成：对村长来说，成功是巩固她的村庄领地；对 Kompas Borneo 来说，是环保政治在地区层面日益增长的合法性；对 WALHI 来说，是基层支持反抗政府强制和企业土地掠夺的实践。然而，村长的故事也需要放在梅拉图斯领导叙述的体裁中考虑；根据我的经验，在这些叙述中，讲述的领导人与授权他或她说话的外部权威之间的每一次会面，并非都在物理上可能发生。既然领导权力由这些与强大外来者的纽带授予，我认识的每位领袖都会讲述与地区权威的会面，因为社群理想地围绕这个故事的力量形成。究竟发生了什么？这个问题在我从那位有魅力、强有力的哥哥那里听到的故事中更加令人困惑；他像妹妹一样把自己置于行动中心，从未提到另一个人。以下是片段：

I went to the timber camp boss to complain about their destruction of our fruit and honey trees and rattan. The boss said, “Take your complaints to Ibu Tien [New Order President Suharto’s wife]. We have permission from the top.” I was angry. I gave that boss half an hour to agree to negotiate with us.
我去木材营地找老板，投诉他们毁坏我们的果树、蜜树和藤。老板说：“把你的投诉带给蒂恩夫人〔新秩序总统苏哈托的妻子〕。我们有上面的许可。”我生气了。我给那个老板半小时，让他同意与我们谈判。
After half an hour, he was still unwilling to talk.
半小时后，他仍不愿谈。
So I went to Jakarta, I went to President Suharto, and I asked, “Is it true that you have agreed to the timber companies cutting down our village trees?”
于是我去雅加达，去见苏哈托总统，我问：“你真的同意木材公司砍倒我们村庄的树木吗？”

The president said, “They are selling my name.” He paid all my expenses to come back; I could have asked for any amount. I’m only sorry I didn’t ask for one of those plastic cards that allows you to take money from a bank whenever you want for the rest of your life. He would have given it to me. Then the journalists from seventeen countries came to Manggur [This is the meeting I have been describing], and they gave their witness to the things I said. That's what helped us close down the timber concession and return the land to the village.
总统说：“他们在卖我的名字。”他支付了我回来的全部费用；我本可以要求任何数额。我只是遗憾没有要一张那种塑料卡，让你余生随时可以从银行取钱。他会给我的。然后来自17个国家的记者来到芒古尔〔这就是我一直描述的那次会议〕，他们为我所说的事作证。这就是帮助我们停止这片特许区的伐木经营并把土地还给村庄的原因。

Is there any Meratus Dayak who could go to Jakarta and meet with the president? No one I spoke with in the province or the capital could even imagine the possibility. From their perspective, it isn’t something village people do. It didn’t happen.
有哪个梅拉图斯达雅克人能去雅加达会见总统吗？我在省里或首都交谈过的人，连这种可能性都无法想象。从他们的角度看，这不是村民会做的事。它没有发生。

I don’t think I have to decide. Through whatever combination of leadership strategies and storytelling, Manggur has thrived. Furthermore, the stories have proliferated into documents. Most astounding perhaps, is a typed page signed by the leader I just quoted. The document uses all the appropriate jargon: “We, the people of Manggur, are indigenous people who protect the environment with our traditional culture. We will consider any offense against the environment to be an offense against our human rights.” I don’t know who wrote this document. When I read it, I had just written a document in the name of another Meratus leader, so I did not think its international literacy completely odd. It surely is a serious mimicry of authoritative rhetoric, and of the most impressive sort. Through just this kind of mimicry, Manggur has become a real village, by which I mean the kind of village other people imagine, rather than just a flexible, tentative Meratus settlement. Indeed, Manggur has become a minor ecotourist attraction, part of the international, national, and regional circuit that draws visitors to villages in the rainforest (Tsing 1999).

我认为我不必作出判断。无论通过怎样的领导策略和讲故事组合，芒古尔兴旺了起来。此外，这些故事还增殖为文件。也许最令人震惊的，是一张我刚才引述的那位领袖签名的打印页。文件使用了所有恰当的术语：“我们芒古尔人民是以传统文化保护环境的原住民。我们将把任何对环境的侵害视为对我们人权的侵犯。”我不知道是谁写了这份文件。我读到它时，刚以另一位梅拉图斯领袖的名义写完一份文件，所以并不觉得它的国际读写能力完全奇怪。它确实是对权威修辞的严肃模仿，而且是最令人印象深刻的那种。正是通过这种模仿，芒古尔变成了一个真实的村庄，我指的是别人想象的那种村庄，而不只是一个灵活、暂定的梅拉图斯定居点。确实，芒古尔已成为一个小型生态旅游景点，成为把游客吸引到雨林村庄的国际、国家和区域环路的一部分（Tsing 1999）。

In the process of making this real village, the landscape also changed. In 1994, it was hard to deny that Manggur’s forest was a model of community-based resource management, quite of the sort that progressive funding agencies have begun to advocate in recent years. As hundreds of ecologically minded visitors, including myself, can attest—and I counted 592 visitors in the guest book between July 1988 and July 1994—Manggur people are happy to explain their customary territory and to point out and identify the diversity of forest plants within it, the areas of mature forest that are not normally cut, and the prohibitions against unreasonable profit from harvesting timber products. Other Meratus also value vegetational diversity, maintain mature forest, and sell almost no timber. But because of the tentativeness through which communities can be defined, it is hard to know whether they fit environmentalists’ criteria for community-based management or not. In contrast, Manggur created the landscape of international environmentalist desire.

在制造这个真实村庄的过程中，地景也改变了。1994年，很难否认芒古尔的森林是以社群为基础的资源管理典范，正是进步资助机构近年来开始倡导的那种。正如数百位有生态意识的访客——包括我自己——可以证明的那样（我在1988年7月至1994年7月的访客簿上数到592位访客），芒古尔人乐于解释他们依习惯法划定的领地，指出并识别其中的森林植物多样性、通常不砍伐的成熟森林区域，以及禁止从采伐木材产品中获取不合理利润的规定。其他梅拉图斯人也重视植被多样性、维护成熟森林，并且几乎不卖木材。但由于社群界定的暂定性，很难知道他们是否符合环保主义者对以社群为基础的管理标准。相比之下，芒古尔创造了国际环保主义者欲望中的地景。

Manggur has not done this by being the right kind of community all along. Instead, a number of smart leaders copied the rhetoric and symbolism of a particular sector of authority, hoping to draw and maintain a constituency with the legitimacy and aura they gained in this process. Their collaboration with SKEPHI, WALHI, and Kompas Borneo did not stem from common understandings of village community or forest history. Instead, they overlapped in understandings about the authority of knowledge and policy emanating from regional and national centers. Manggur people agreed with those from the province and the capital that elites make the rules. It is in this context that Manggur leaders almost surely prompted Kompas Borneo members to include development rhetoric in their grant proposal. Development is the wisdom of the state, and Manggur leaders took that on in the same ways they take on environmentalist wisdom.

芒古尔做到这一点，并非因为它一直都是正确的那种社群。相反，一群聪明的领袖复制了某一权威部门的修辞和象征，希望凭借在此过程中获得的合法性和光环来吸引并维持支持者。他们与 SKEPHI、WALHI 和 Kompas Borneo 的协作，并非源于对村庄社群或森林史的共同理解。相反，他们的理解叠合在于来自地区和全国中心的知识与政策权威。芒古尔人与省和首都的人一致认为，精英制定规则。正是在这种背景下，芒古尔领袖几乎肯定促使 Kompas Borneo 成员在资助申请中加入了发展修辞。发展是国家的智慧，芒古尔领袖接受它，就像他们接受环保主义智慧一样。

Just a fifteen-minute hike from the central settlement of Manggur is another Meratus hamlet, a part of Manggur village. The people I talked to there were extremely eager to talk to me about other things, yet they told me that they knew nothing about how the timber concession was closed. They told me to talk with the leaders I have mentioned; that story is those leaders’ business, they said. The events in Manggur were not a grassroots movement in the ordinary sense. They did not unite the people of the village in a common resistance. When I asked a Meratus friend in another district what had happened to the timber concession, he said the village head of Manggur was able to get help from important connections that allowed her to influence the officials. The borrowed authority of leaders, rather than unified community action, is the dominant Meratus model of political agency. It is hard to argue that it is wrong in describing this case.

距芒古尔中心定居点仅十五分钟步行路程，是另一个梅拉图斯小村，属于芒古尔村的一部分。我在那里交谈的人非常渴望与我谈别的事，然而他们告诉我，他们对伐木特许区的经营是如何被叫停的一无所知。他们让我去跟我提到过的领袖谈；他们说，那个故事是那些领袖的事。芒古尔的事件不是通常意义上的基层运动。它们没有把村庄的人民团结在共同抵抗中。当我问另一个区的梅拉图斯朋友伐木特许区发生了什么时，他说芒古尔村长能够从重要关系中获得帮助，使她能够影响官员。领袖借来的权威，而不是统一的社群行动，是梅拉图斯政治能动性的主导模式。很难说这种描述对本案是错误的。

These last Meratus stories remind us that despite its collaborative stability, the community-managed forest of Manggur had a rather tentative status. Meratus community members can undermine the best-laid plans of leaders like those who helped bring Manggur’s community-managed forest into being. In general, they do this not so much by destroying the forest as by refusing to act like a community.
最后这几个梅拉图斯故事提醒我们，尽管芒古尔的社群管理森林具有协作稳定性，它的状态却相当不稳固。梅拉图斯社群成员可以破坏领袖最周密的计划，包括那些帮助促成芒古尔社群管理森林的人的计划。总的来说，他们这样做与其说是通过毁坏森林，不如说是通过拒绝像社群那样行动。

Furthermore, although the emergence of the community-managed forest in Manggur was locally important and effective, it did not travel anywhere, in part because few of the parties involved knew just how well this environmental “exercise” had worked. When I spoke with Meratus in other places in the 1990s about how they might deal with timber company incursions, no one imagined that they might apply the Manggur exercise to their own situation. When urban activists returned to mount a campaign against logging in 1999, they re-invented community-managed forests based on their knowledge of other places.
此外，尽管芒古尔社群管理森林的出现在当地重要而有效，它并未传播到任何地方，部分因为涉及其中的各方很少知道这次环境“演练”究竟有多成功。20世纪90年代我在其他地方与梅拉图斯人谈论如何应对木材公司入侵时，没有人想象他们可以把芒古尔演练应用于自己的处境。1999年城市活动家回来发起反伐木运动时，他们根据对其他地方的了解重新发明了社群管理森林。

Yet the very limitations of the incident make it easy to think with as a model of the effectiveness of collaboration. It is possible to tell the story in its own historical bubble, with no succeeding history to undermine the promise of the initial emergence of the category. The story tells of possibility and of hope. Sometimes difference can lead to new forms of unity and struggle.
然而，正是这一事件的局限，使它容易作为一个协作有效性的模型来思考。可以在它自身的历史气泡中讲述这个故事，没有后续历史来削弱这一范畴最初出现时的承诺。这个故事讲述可能性与希望。有时差异可以通向团结与斗争的新形式。

Progressive activists spend most of their time either searching for seamless consensus or making a point of their irreconcilable differences. My story suggests other political avenues. It also suggests other methods for learning about the world.
进步活动家大部分时间要么在寻找无缝共识，要么在强调自己不可调和的分歧。我的故事暗示其他政治途径。它也暗示了解世界的其他方法。
Thus, for example, research objectives:

For most advocates of environmentalism, the challenge for scholars of the environment is to learn to gather compatible data sets so that we can aggregate the data to form a global picture. The issue of local perspectives, from this point of view, is a technical problem to be overcome. My story gives space for the opposite approach. What if we paid more attention to incompatible data sets? In other words, what if we took a look at the ways social position, genre, and practical knowledge shape the data we gather? Instead of erasing incompatibility, we need to find out where it makes a difference.
因此，举例来说，研究目标：
对大多数环保主义倡导者来说，环境学者面临的挑战是学会收集相容的数据集，以便我们能聚合数据，形成全球图景。从这个观点看，地方视角的问题是一个需要克服的技术问题。我的故事为相反的方法留出空间。如果我们更关注不相容的数据集呢？换句话说，如果我们审视社会位置、体裁和实践知识塑造我们所收集数据的方式呢？与其抹除不相容性，我们需要找出它在何处产生差异。

Banjarmasin, Jakarta, and Manggur activists tell different histories of the forest: the forest is a challenging wild place; the forest is a site of popular resistance and communal management; the forest is the medium of social networking. These stories do not fit together neatly; they allow us to gather different kinds of data about resources and resource management as well as different stories of environmental activism to save forests. It is only through recognizing this kind of discrepancy that we can begin to sketch the environmental history of this area. Furthermore, this history is not served by just setting these perspectives side by side. The hierarchy that sponsors but does not control their divergence, and the contingent overlaps and collaborations that mark out their effects, are essential parts of that history. Indeed, the natural objects that populate that history—including community forests, villages, and environmental advocates of various sorts—become historical agents precisely through the contingent collaborations that show us their agency from varied perspectives.

班贾尔马辛、雅加达和芒古尔的活动家讲述不同的森林史：森林是一个充满挑战的荒野之地；森林是民众抵抗与社群管理的场所；森林是社会网络的媒介。这些故事并不整齐地拼合；它们让我们能够收集关于资源和资源管理的不同数据，以及关于拯救森林的环保行动主义的不同故事。只有通过承认这种差异，我们才能开始描绘这个地区的环境史。此外，仅仅把这些视角并置，并不能服务于这段历史。促成却不控制其分歧的等级体系，以及标记其效果的偶然重叠与协作，都是这段历史的基本部分。确实，填充这段历史的自然对象——包括社群森林、村庄和各种环保倡导者——正是通过偶然的协作而成为历史行动者，这些协作从不同视角向我们展示其能动性。
Beyond Manggur
超越芒古尔
What happens when these categories gain the power to travel?
当这些范畴获得旅行的力量时，会发生什么？

My own story of what happened in Manggur, like those I have been relating, began as a particularly positioned oral narrative. I designed the story for academic settings, but before long it carried me into contact with program officers from the Ford Foundation, which by the 1990s had become a center for many such stories about what had come to be called community-based natural resource management. (The awkward acronym is CBNRM.) Through its Rural Poverty Alleviation Program, the Ford Foundation had become a major funder of CBNRM projects around the world—including one submitted by the members of Kompas Borneo to work in Manggur. The Ford Foundation has a reflexive streak, and program officers tend to enjoy hearing scholarly analyses of their programs. My Manggur story caught someone’s attention in this regard, and for the next few years through conferences and workshops I found myself with access to a host of other related stories about community-managed forests, fisheries, wildlife, water projects, and the like. Mingling under the auspices of the Ford Foundation, these concepts were no longer just local sparks of hope; they stretched, worried each other, and traveled.

我自己关于芒古尔发生什么的故事，像我一直在讲述的那些故事一样，始于一个特定位置的口述叙事。我为学术场合设计这个故事，但不久它就把我带入与福特基金会项目官员的接触；到20世纪90年代，福特基金会已成为许多这类故事的汇集中心，这些故事关于后来所谓的以社群为基础的自然资源管理（其缩写 CBNRM 颇为别扭）。通过其农村减贫项目，福特基金会已成为世界各地 CBNRM 项目的主要资助者——包括 Kompas Borneo 成员提交的在芒古尔工作的项目。福特基金会有一种反思倾向，项目官员往往喜欢听对其项目的学术分析。我的芒古尔故事在这方面引起了某人的注意，在接下来的几年里，通过会议和工作坊，我接触到了大量关于社群管理森林、渔业、野生动物、水利项目等的其他相关故事。在福特基金会的主持下交融，这些概念不再只是地方性的希望火花；它们延伸、相互扰动，并旅行。

One of the first things I learned was that the excitement about community resource management at Ford drew from contingencies—rather as it had in Manggur. Once suggested, CBNRM filled a niche that had not been noticed before. It stretched between community empowerment and conservation. It fulfilled dreams of improvement as well as preservation. The idea developed, too, when it found unexpected collaborators, inexplicably drawn to each other by this small corroboration in their otherwise independent agendas.

The emergence of the concept at Ford resembled its moment in Manggur; yet, of course, the Ford Foundation and a short if successful gathering in an obscure Meratus village could not be more different. In Manggur, participants glimpsed the promise of community forests in the light brush of contact. No bureaucratic or commercial institutionalization marred the protean possibilities of the dream. In contrast, the goal of the Ford Foundation is to make such promising visions real—with all the power and peril of that exercise.
我最早学到的事情之一是，福特对社群资源管理的兴奋源自偶然——颇像在芒古尔那样。一旦被提出，CBNRM 就填补了一个此前未被注意的生态位。它延伸于社群赋权与保护之间。它实现了改善与保存的梦想。这个观念也在找到意外的合作者时发展起来，这些合作者被各自独立议程中的这一小小印证莫名地相互吸引。
这个概念在福特的出现类似于它在芒古尔的时刻；然而，福特基金会和一个偏僻梅拉图斯村庄中短暂却成功的聚会当然再不同不过。在芒古尔，参与者在接触的轻轻擦碰中瞥见了社群森林的承诺。没有官僚或商业的制度化玷污梦想多变的可能性。相比之下，福特基金会的目标是让这些有希望的愿景成真——带着这种做法的一切权力和危险。

The Ford Foundation’s promotion of CBNRM gave it the kind of universal status I began this book by discussing—the status of a universal-in-engagement. On the one hand, Ford’s power and money urged NGO workers and activists from around the world to recast their projects within the emergent rhetoric of community resource management. On the other hand, each project was marked by its specific set of more or less self-conscious overlaps and compromises among collaborators. In contrast to many well-promoted globalist concepts, CBNRM is supposed to have a local flavor, and so it is important to remain suspicious of claims for local originality, which may only support a program’s self-justification. Every international conference on the topic—however much a celebration of diversity—teaches NGO workers, as well as academics, how to cast their projects with a pitch that might get them a grant. When Ford Foundation program officers are around, participants are busy pitching standard lines. Yet when grantees go home, they must work these lines into the matrix of possibilities offered by their practical situation.

福特基金会对 CBNRM 的推广赋予它一种我在本书开头讨论过的普遍地位——作为介入性的普遍性的地位。一方面，福特的权力和金钱敦促世界各地的非政府组织工作人员和活动家，用社群资源管理的新兴修辞重新表述他们的项目。另一方面，每个项目都带有其特定的、或多或少自觉的合作者重叠与妥协。与许多大力推广的全球主义概念不同，CBNRM 本应具有地方风味，因此重要的是对地方原创性的主张保持怀疑，这些主张可能只支持项目自我辩护。每一场关于该主题的国际会议——无论多么庆祝多样性——都在教导非政府组织工作人员和学者如何以可能获得资助的调门来包装项目。福特基金会项目官员在场时，参与者忙于推销标准话术。然而当受资助者回家，他们必须把这些话术编织进实际处境所提供的可能性矩阵。

With the funds and legitimacy the Ford Foundation offers, grantees have the opportunity to show that their dreams can work in the world. Utopian critique meets realpolitik here. Projects must position themselves in relation to government bureaucracies and commercial and policy elites. New and often unsavory collaborators must be entertained. The original dream may lose its force. The question of co-optation is ever present.
有了福特基金会提供的资金和合法性，受资助者有机会证明他们的梦想可以在世界上奏效。乌托邦批评在此遇见现实政治。项目必须在与政府官僚机构以及商业和政策精英的关系中定位自己。必须应付新的、往往令人不快的合作者。原初梦想可能失去力量。收编的问题始终存在。

As projects develop supporters and opponents, the influence of the donor organization itself sparks contention. Did projects develop their ideas of “community” only to meet the standards of potential grant agencies?

When “community” is dreamed up and imposed by outsiders, what happens to local assessments and dreams? Issues of scale-making are crucial. “Communities” are constituted in relation to other kinds of scale-making projects, including bureaucracies, nations, and international bodies of power and expertise. Community-making projects may or may not empower local people; it all depends on just how this relation is organized. Who benefits?
随着项目发展出支持者和反对者，捐助组织本身的影响也引发争论。项目发展“社群”观念，只是为了满足潜在资助机构的标准吗？
当“社群”被外来者构想并强加时，地方的评估和梦想会怎样？尺度制造的问题至关重要。“社群”是相对于其他类型的尺度制造项目——包括官僚机构、民族国家以及国际权力与专业知识机构——而被构成的。社群制造项目可能赋权当地人，也可能不；一切都取决于这种关系如何被组织。谁受益？

Rather than deliver a definitive policy assessment of these questions, Ford Foundation program officers working with CBNRM participated in a series of discussions involving academics and advocates, as well as bureaucrats and donor organizations. The discussions in which I participated were challenging. In the late 1990s, scholarly trends were moving away from an endorsement of activist projects and experiments. Practitioners and scholars often gravitated to different styles for discussing programs. Where practitioners focused on the strengths and weaknesses of particular projects, scholars tended to place these projects in longer histories and wider geographies of knowledge and power. Scholars pointed out that “native communities” are generally imagined within colonial legacies of segregation and racism. These legacies can limit the options for village people, denying them the privileges of full citizenship. Meanwhile, government and international management programs can use community-building exercises to discipline rural people, urging them to comply with barely relevant expert orthodoxies “for their own good.” These perspectives usefully enlarged the context in which we were able to discuss particular projects. At the same time, they dampened the spirit of advocacy, making those who wanted to change the world seem self-aggrandizing, if effective, or silly, if not.

福特基金会从事 CBNRM 的项目官员没有对这些问题作出决定性的政策评估，而是参与了一系列讨论，涉及学者、倡导者、官僚和捐助组织。我参与的讨论很有挑战性。20世纪90年代末，学术潮流正从对行动主义项目和实验的认可转向别处。实践者和学者常常倾向于用不同风格讨论项目。实践者关注特定项目的长处与弱点，学者则倾向于把这些项目放入更长的历史和更广的知识与权力地理中。学者指出，“原住民社群”一般是在殖民遗留的隔离与种族主义中被想象的。这些遗产可能限制村民的选择，剥夺他们完整公民身份的特权。与此同时，政府和国际管理机构可以利用社群建设演练来规训乡村人民，敦促他们“为了自己好”而服从几乎不相关的专家正统。这些视角有用地扩大了我们讨论特定项目的语境。同时，它们抑制了倡导精神，使那些想改变世界的人显得自我膨胀——如果有效的话——或者显得愚蠢——如果无效的话。

In the process of discussion, I found myself provoked to think differently. On the one hand, scholarly colleagues challenged me to consider the real dangers of too easy a generosity toward programs for “community” empowerment. On the other hand, community advocates made me consider whether scholarship had stopped working well as a public interlocutor. These concerns come to a head in the task of assessing the populist and romantic commitments of middle-class urban young people such as those who gathered once in Manggur. Certainly, their commitments embody the ambivalent legacies of the concept of “community.” Are these young people part of the problem or part of the solution?
在讨论过程中，我发现自己被促使以不同方式思考。一方面，学者同事挑战我考虑过于轻易地宽待“社群”赋权项目所蕴含的真实危险。另一方面，社群倡导者让我考虑，学术是否已不再作为公共对话者良好运作。这些关切在评估曾聚集在芒古尔的那类中产阶级城市青年的民粹主义和浪漫承诺这一任务中达到顶点。当然，他们的承诺体现了“社群”概念矛盾重重的遗产。这些年轻人是问题的一部分，还是解决方案的一部分？

To return to these particular protagonists helps to clarify the challenge. Community resource management is a charismatic idea; it is easily co-opted by powerful institutions and bureaucracies. The worst situations are those in which local options are foreclosed by the force of institutions. For example, the popularity of the concept has recommended it to the international agencies that implement structural adjustment programs. Why not use community labor to save public money while dangling the hope for community autonomy as a device to keep the populace in line? German-run forestry projects in The Gambia, in West Africa, have adopted just this perspective, according to analyst Richard Schroeder (1999). In one project, communities take over a schedule of forest labor dictated from above with the promise that after three years of good behavior, they may qualify to apply for land tenure.

回到这些特定主角有助于澄清挑战。社群资源管理是一个富有感召力的观念；它容易被强大的机构和官僚机构收编。最糟的情况是地方选择被制度的力量封闭。例如，这一概念的流行使其被推荐给实施结构调整项目的国际机构。为什么不利用社群劳动节省公共资金，同时把社群自治的希望悬在那里，作为让民众守规矩的手段？分析者理查德·施罗德（Richard Schroeder，1999）指出，西非冈比亚的德国经营的林业项目就采取了这种视角。在一个项目中，社群接管了一份自上而下规定的森林劳动时间表，并得到承诺：表现良好三年后，他们可能有资格申请土地保有权。

The distinction between well-meaning community advocates and crassly manipulative institutions blurs, however, when we consider how village elites may remake themselves as interlocutors for international expertise.

In their cosmopolitan efforts to connect with powerful outsiders, village leaders may endorse forms of knowledge that are wrong or biased when considered in the context of local practices. Manggur elders have been quite capable in making their stories about the Manggur forest work to match middle-class dreams—and in the process, further their own leadership strategies. Moreover, not every local vision of “community” extends social justice or environmental protection. Some visions only build a small network of privilege. There are no simple standards of assessment here. The only way to think about the political potential of a project is to learn about its local dynamics, on the one hand, and its attempts to reach out to wider collaborators, on the other.
然而，当我们考虑村庄精英如何可能把自己重塑为国际专业知识的对话者时，善意的社群倡导者与粗暴操纵的机构之间的区分就模糊了。

在联系强大外来者的世界主义努力中，村庄领袖可能认可那些放在当地实践语境中看是错误或有偏见的知识形式。芒古尔长者相当有能力让关于芒古尔森林的故事配合中产阶级的梦想——并在此过程中推进自己的领导策略。此外，并非每种地方“社群”愿景都扩展社会正义或环境保护。有些愿景只是建立一个小的特权网络。这里没有简单的评估标准。思考一个项目政治潜力的唯一方式，一方面了解其地方动态，另一方面了解其联系更广泛合作者的尝试。

But this is where the best and the most critically aware scholarship fails us. Theory has followed its own specifications. In overcoming the parochialism of the case study, theory overreaches to show each local situation as nothing more than an exemplification of a self-fulfilling global scheme. As long as this is what counts as theory, we have trouble getting either to urgent local dilemmas or to far-reaching collaborative visions. In assessing environmental politics, theory has had less and less to say to activists, visionaries, and the public at large. This is because theory, in directing itself to prophetic futures, has addressed itself more to replication and planned development than to unexpected opportunities and injuries that must be addressed, however inadequately. We can do better.

但这正是最好、最具批判意识的学术让我们失望之处。理论遵循自身的规范。在克服个案研究的偏狭时，理论过度伸展，把每种地方情境都展示为自我实现的全球方案的一个例证。只要这仍被视作理论，我们就既难以触及紧迫的地方困境，也难以触及深远的协作愿景。在评估环境政治时，理论对活动家、愿景家和广大公众能说的话越来越少。这是因为理论在指向预言式未来时，更多面向复制与计划发展，而不是必须应对——无论多么不充分——的意外机会与伤害。我们可以做得更好。

Theories of globalization have been particularly bad in this regard. Because they lay out inevitable trajectories, they cannot appreciate either the contingency of nightmares or the promise of utopian critique. Why did anyone bother to claim community forests in Manggur? Corporate theft and destruction made a response urgent. That Manggur leaders were able to reach out to tap the fantasies of provincial nature lovers and national activists was a local victory. It also launched a broader vision of hope: the hope that forests could be sustained as a source of life for multiple humans and nonhumans—and not just distant corporations.
全球化理论在这方面尤其糟糕。因为它们铺陈不可避免的轨迹，所以既不能领会噩梦的偶然性，也不能领会乌托邦批评的承诺。为什么有人要不厌其烦地在芒古尔主张社群森林？公司的盗窃与破坏使回应变得紧迫。芒古尔领袖能够伸手利用省里的自然爱好者和全国活动家的幻想，这是一场地方胜利。它还启动了一个更广阔的希望愿景：希望森林可以作为众多人类与非人类生命的源泉而持续存在——而不只是远方公司的源泉。

Finding hope has become more difficult in recent years. As illegal resource extraction booms, it becomes harder to imagine community representatives who want anything other than their share of the money. During the New Order, resource rents mainly bypassed local residents; when the regime fell, many forest-dwellers were willing to fight for their forests. Now payments are distributed more widely. As one businessman is said to have quipped, “In Sukarno’s day, we paid under the table. In Suharto’s day, we paid over the table. Now they’ve taken away the table” (Iverleigh 2003: 26). Everyone is free to demand a cut.
近年来寻找希望变得更加困难。随着非法资源开采繁荣，越来越难想象想要别的东西——除了自己那份钱——的社群代表。新秩序时期，资源租金主要绕过当地居民；政权倒台后，许多森林居民愿意为森林而战。现在款项分配得更广。据说一位商人打趣道：“苏加诺时代，我们在桌子底下付钱。苏哈托时代，我们在桌子上面付钱。现在他们把桌子拿走了”（Iverleigh 2003: 26）。人人都可以自由要求分一杯羹。

Yet the more difficult the community forestry exercise becomes, the more necessary it seems. Otherwise we resign ourselves to forest plantations with privatized security—or to total destruction of the forest and its livelihoods. The international experts have already given up. The only ones who still bother to struggle over these issues are activists, students, and nature lovers—and the rural communities with whom they interface. This seems a particularly bad time to use scholarly prediction to denigrate their efforts.
然而，社群林业实践越困难，似乎就越必要。否则我们就只能认命于带私有化安保的森林种植园——或者森林及其生计的彻底毁灭。国际专家已经放弃。仍然愿意为这些问题费心斗争的，只有活动家、学生和自然爱好者——以及与他们接触的乡村社群。这似乎是一个特别糟糕的时机，用学术预测来贬低他们的努力。
To ignore utopian potential is not just pessimistic; it is also historically misleading. Insightful criticism has somehow turned to abstract dogma.
忽视乌托邦潜力不只是悲观；在历史意义上也具有误导性。富有洞见的批评不知何故变成了抽象教条。

How has it happened that in order to stay true to hopes for a more livable earth, one must turn away from scholarly theory? Dialogues across scholar-practitioner lines—such as those the Ford Foundation has supported—are an invitation to come up with something rather different. Might it be possible to use other scholarly skills, including the ability to tell a story that both acknowledges imperial power and leaves room for possibility?
怎么会发生这样的情况：为了忠于对一个更宜居地球的希望，一个人必须背离学术理论？跨越学者—实践者界线的对话——例如福特基金会支持的对话——是提出完全不同东西的邀请。是否可能运用其他学术技能，包括讲述一个既承认帝国权力又为可能性留出空间的故事的能力？
Re-engaging Theory
重新介入理论

This book has suggested how one might tell these other stories. I have shown the importance of attention to situated dilemmas, on the one hand, and the moving current of human empathy we call the universal, on the other. To capture this duality, I have focused on the engagement of universals.
本书已提示如何讲述这些其他故事。我一方面展示关注情境化困境的重要性，另一方面展示我们称为普遍物的人类同理心流动的重要性。为捕捉这种二元性，我聚焦于普遍性的介入。

Despite the standardization and consolidation of capitalism, I found it impossible to learn about resource extraction without dragging my analysis into the arrogance and despair of the Kalimantan frontier.
